By utilizing a dynamic head, we're capable of estimating the parameters of the transformation and synthesizing videos from any angle. Our approach enables accurate novel viewpoint prediction, as demonstrated in our experiments across multiple datasets.

We experimentally create a phase beam splitter using higher-order photonic modes, combining a waveguide coupler and length-varying photonic crystal waveguide sections. This innovation enables the conversion of intensity couplers into functional beam splitters capable of manipulating higher-order photonic modes. Our findings provide a means to convert between these types of devices and can be applied to transform lossy systems into unitary transformations.

Using an effective relativistic two-body formalism, we apply modified rotating gluon bags to derive resonance mass spectra for $B_{q\bar{s}}$ baryons in their $J^+ = 0,1,2$ pseudoscalar, scalar, and tensor configurations. Our approach incorporates relevant three-body approximations to ensure the model's validity. Comparing our calculated masses with experimental values and prior theoretical approaches demonstrates generally satisfactory results, although tensor masses are slightly overestimated. Notably, our approach enables separate analysis of the influences of three-body relativistic effects, bag dynamics, and angular momentum rotations on tensor masses, which are significantly higher than their pseudoscalar and scalar counterparts.

A simplified well-mixed model for aerosol dispersion has been applied to a real-world classroom setting to analyze the distribution of aerosol particles. By using actual measurement data from specific locations within the room, a precise fit to model predictions was achieved, allowing an estimate of the ventilation exchange rate. An estimate of virus particle concentration over time has also been derived, and key factors that limit predictive accuracy have been discussed. A comparison with a complex two-compartment model and measurements from another study has been made, and although a simplified model does not fully capture local airflow patterns, it has been found to effectively predict virus particle concentration around an infected person in this localized environment.

We investigated the layer-dependent Hall effect within cobaltedbismuth multilayers, focusing on the scattering mechanism associated with interfacesthan bulk. Varying the thickness of the Bismuth layers enables us to control the density of states in relation to the scattering of current-carrying states at the interfacesthan in the bulk. The results show that the Hall angle reaches a peak when the Fermi level is close to the density of states threshold in the Bismuth layers. The results also suggest that the Hall angle can be used to study the scattering of the ifeosthan in the bulk. The results may have significant implications for the development of high sensitivity Hall angle probes.

We analyze the $p$-dimensional fractional Schrödinger equation in N dimensions, a problem involving a nonlinear nonlinear term |$\partial_p$u|$^{alpha}$, a spherical Schrödinger equation can be reduced to a one-dimensional nonlinear equation |$\partial_p$u|$^{alpha}$, which is a note on the influence of the parameter $\alpha$. When $\alpha$ is greater than one, a new change of variables is used, a asymptotic expansion of the solution is derived as $p$ approaches infinity. For 2-dimensional cases, a numerical verification of the asymptotic behavior is performed. When $\alpha$ is less than or equal to one, the asymptotic form of the solution is also-paired.

We investigate how restricting the $p$-norm Lipschitz continuous property of a neural network affects its empirical performance. With a focus on classification tasks, we introduce and examine a optimized model that breaks the typical performance trend associated with the $p$-norm value. We develop a neural network that can achieve any valid level of Lipschitz continuity in the specified norm without compromising empirical performance. We then conduct various experiments to determine if this model comes with any disadvantages in terms of generalization or slowness in training. Surprisingly, we found that penalizing the gradient flow during training does not result in significant slowdown or overfitting in networks trained with a bounded Lipschitz constant.

Recurring background mimicking vector leptoquark signals in search for them in the top-antitop quark category in the LHC's proton-proton collisions could potentially be minimized by improving the leptoquark simulation. This is especially pertinent for scalar and vector types of leptoquarks that decay into an antiproton and a positron or an antineutron and a positive pion, searching for which in the antitop quark sector is characteristic. We show that adopting the next-to-leading order plus fixed number of partons method for these rare occurrences might be achievable and results in harder jet momentum distributions compared to the default approach, yielding a harder tail in the antiproton (or antineutron) momentum distribution that could easily be missed in the current analysis. These results are applicable to other leptoquark types that decay into hadrons and antitop quarks and are also relevant to searches for quantum gravity effects.

Although deep learning techniques have seen significant progression in low-dose PET image reconstruction, using such large models often results in excessive computation consumption and reduced image quality due to unavoidable substitutions in the reconstruction process. In response, we present a compressed deep neural network framework that minimizes overhead while maintaining high performance, specifically for PET/MRI fusion. This compact network is composed of multiple stages, incorporating attention mechanisms, graph neural network components, and dictionary learning, which can be executed without substitution when integrated into the Kittler-Rosec acceleration loop. This streamlined design enables adequate sufficient-statistic achievement with modest overhead, resulting in a practical and efficient solution. Our experimental data shows that the proposed network can produce images of superior quality to those from using the original deep neural network models, while consuming reduced computation time and memory. This efficiency allows the proposed network to be executed on the clinical PET/MRI scanner.

To assess the influence of state-of-the-art neural coreference resolution models' ability to capture the contextual essence of language, as proposed by centering theory, we examined the effectiveness of various context-independent and context-based neural coreference resolution approaches when applied to the featural analysis of text. Our experiments revealed that the use of basic embedding techniques and context-based analysis significantly enhance the explanatory power of theoretical frameworks in understanding complex language structures. Specifically, our results showed that context-based embeddings significantly strengthen the ability to capture linguistic features relevant to coreference resolution tasks, as predicted by the principles of grammatical theory.

The growth of portable devices with WiFi capability can facilitate real-time location determination through these devices by analyzing signal strength through WiFi signals. Although this method is effective, it struggles with accuracy in certain environments due to various sources of noise that affect WiFi signals. To improve the reliability of location data derived from WiFi fingerprints in a given region, we employed machine learning algorithms for more precise estimation of ground distance between signals. Using real-world test results from two environments, we found that models trained on signal data from one setting could successfully apply their data processing techniques to another setting with comparable accuracy, revealing the robustness of our approach. Furthermore, we demonstrated that even when applying these processing methods to signals from different frequency ranges, we could estimate ground distance with a mean error of 1.54 meters and a maximum error of 3.69 meters, revealing the adaptability of our model.

When a high-energy beam enters a high-vacuum beamline for multiple uses, the beam interacts with the surrounding electromagnetic waves in a complex manner across various time intervals and frequency ranges. To better understand the effects of this interaction, particularly the point when beam self-stability overcomes the constraints imposed by the laws of physics, researchers are examining various scenarios that the beam might encounter as it travels through the beamline for multiple cycles. By simulating different patterns of beam filling using a specialized computational tool, researchers can dissect the complex interaction between the beam and electromagnetic waves, and how different patterns influence the minimum beam density required for the beam to remain stable. Through these simulations, three distinct patterns have been identified and compared, including one that aligns with the binary code used in cache storage systems, providing valuable insights for optimizing future experimental designs.

Researchers studying the double-color-entropy variance (CEV) for two-gluon interactions in QCD found the results match exactly with the amplitude of six O(Nc) cyclical soft gluons in the theory's classical limit. These matches hold for both total and Regge-triple contributions under specific conditions. The CEV for two-gluon interactions can be represented as the product of two factors, one of which aligns with the trace of a combination of fundamental matrices in SU(Nc), while the other, unknown part, could be associated with the potential energy of six-gluon interactions in the collinear limit. This part might contribute positively to the anomalous dimension of the null cusp.

The free energy of polymer brushes stretched across curved surfaces can equal that of a flat surface starting from a specific curvature threshold, as predicted by the mean curvature approximation. The brush resides on the surface of a curved cylinder with two distinct monomer density regions, either symmetric or asymmetric, as opposed to the classic bimodal density profile seen on flat surfaces. The transition between these density regions, known as the interface, shifts from the inner to the outer part of the brush, as opposed to surfaces with infinite curvature where interface displacement doesn't occur. The transition density, however, remains unchanged. The shift in interface position is influenced by various parameters, including the polymer chain length, the degree of stretching, the density of contact points, and the thermal energy. The findings from this study have implications for the understanding of polymer behavior on curved surfaces, as well as for the design of block copolymer systems used in nanofabrication processes.

Researchers studying complex graph structures are delving into the relationship between graph distance metrics and their dimensionality after applying various reductions techniques. A key component of their analysis involves a method called the "truncated metric" that alters the way nodes measure their mutual distances beyond a certain threshold. This approach is inspired by real-world applications such as GPS tracking and data clustering algorithms. Their study reveals that graphs where distance is constrained within a specific range have a much lower dimensionality compared to their unconstrained counterparts. In particular, they prove that for some graph types, achieving a reduced dimensionality through this method is impossible, whereas for other types, their proposed algorithm can accurately determine the truncated metric dimension of a given graph.

An in-depth examination of the long-term variability patterns in 11 active galactic nuclei using 10 years of light curves from the Pan-STARRS1 survey. A careful examination of system errors and the effects of missing data, particularly around the new minimum light phase following a supernova explosion in one of the nuclei. Various statistical methods are compared to analyze the nuclei's variability, which reveals that results are heavily influenced by observation frequencies varying over time and not errors associated with photometric measurements. A significant correlation is found between the nuclei's variability and their environmental settings, which are determined using a satellite map.

A well-known result by Young (1994) indicates that the Birkhoff-von Neumann theorem cannot be extended to valuations derived from bipartite matchings in any way other than a trivial interpretation. We contend that this should be viewed as implying the social welfare in decisions made by an optimal mechanism is completely recoverable in the long run. We propose a revised understanding of these valuations by incorporating an external source, implying the Birkhoff-von Neumann theorem cannot be applied in any way other than a trivial interpretation when extended to general settings. We demonstrate that this leads to the conclusion that the social welfare in decisions made by an optimal mechanism is unbounded, indicating it can be arbitrarily lower than the maximum possible. We further investigate a simpler learning algorithm and show that, despite this issue, the social welfare in decisions made by this algorithm is guaranteed to be at least $1/3$ times the true social welfare in the long run.

Several binary asteroid discovery cases have utilized analyses of how light appears to spread across telescopes to a degree, precisely by examining the distribution of brightness for individual objects in images. Previously, studies have focused on single, isolated objects, but new approaches can now be applied to binary asteroids even within wide-area surveys designed to track the motion of celestial bodies over time. To a degree, existing models have utilized sophisticated techniques for determining the movement of objects in space, but simpler alternatives have been proposed that combine general theories of motion with analysis of how objects move across the sky. These theories are supported by empirical observations and involve examining the spread of brightness for each image, as well as additional data from the positions of objects in the sky. Based on this, a new approach is proposed for automatically detecting binary asteroid candidates from video streams of the sky, as well as other scenarios aimed at identifying objects in space. This approach is tested using real-world data from the Pan-STARRS1 survey, as well as simulated images of the sky, and results in evaluating the degree, precisely by examining the spread of brightness for each image, in which objects exist in pairs.

Recent studies in economics have highlighted the significance of peer influence within networks. However, estimating this phenomenon remains challenging due to the lack of exogenous variation in network structures. Utilizing the randomized complete block design commonly applied in agricultural and medical trials, we can isolate the design's block effects as an analogue to peer influence. By applying this design to form a network, researchers can obtain unbiased estimates of network influence, along with standard errors that account for implementation details. We examine various design-based designs, with a focus on the class of design-randomized designs that ensure a uniform level of peer influence among all design nodes, thus providing an ideal setting for analysis. A simulated environment is created to test and compare the effectiveness of different designs and estimation methods.

This paper introduces two efficient chain rule formulas for fractional operators of variable order, yielding more concise and practical expressions that can alternatively be expressed through a Clément–Peetre type inequality and an Ornstein-type formula. We also derive a fractional isoperimetric inequality for a variable-order operator and establish the absolute continuity of a fractional derivative with respect to a variable order. Moreover, an explicit expression for the fractional operator of variable order is obtained in terms of a Riemann-Liouville operator.

Collaborative games with hidden information are effective tools for researching
complex social interactions, and theory-of-mind models can significantly
improve an agent's success in these engagements. While automated approaches like
inverse reinforcement learning can uncover hidden information from observed
behavior, they require precise and comprehensive data, and may fail with subtle
clues. In contrast, a general class of optimal policies based on probability
distributions does not require precise data, but may also require excessive
precision in practice. We introduce a novel paper-unfolding model called
Probabilistic Theory of Mind (PTm) that effectively incorporates probability
distributions, strategic data, and subtle hints, and presents PTm as a
recursive function. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PTm in two settings
with hidden data where it achieves better results than the original model class
and the Backoff Reification (BR) alternative, and also demonstrates its robust
performance when there are variations in the data.

In this paper, we apply topological analysis to identify shallow and deep knots within a category of achiral trefoil knots commonly formed by a 6-bead chain with random bond angles. We classify these knots into pathways based on the sequence of projected knots formed during their creation. Our findings reveal two distinct pathways for forming these knots: one for shallow knots and another for deeply knotted structures. We observe that the pathway to form deeply knotted structures is significantly less common than that for shallow knots. Additionally, we introduce the concept of "folding pathways" by examining the frequencies of projected knots at each step. Our results show that certain projected knots appear more often than others and can serve as preferred stages in the formation of these knots. We discuss how our findings may have implications for understanding the folding processes of biological proteins.

Given any closed symplectic manifold, we can construct a vast number of distinct smooth structures that are compatible with the same underlying topological framework and a single symplectic class, according to a prescribed growth rate.

In a theoretical framework where a new type of matter is present within a strong, non-abelian force field, we explore a way for a massless particle, specifically a Nambu-Goldstone boson, to acquire mass. To illustrate this process, we use a model based on the formation of neutral, electrically uncharged kaons. By deriving an effective potential in a simplified approach that considers only the interaction between bosons in lower angular momentum states, we can analyze the conditions necessary for a phase transition, in this case, where the condensation of particles leads to mass generation. However, a more thorough examination using a relativistic, quark, and meson mixing model reveals that the condensation primarily occurs in the scalar, not pseudoscalar, sector. This discrepancy reveals that the acquisition of mass in the Standard Model, such as the mass of the pion, may not be explained by a phase transition and the resulting condensation of particles.

Training models that excel in scenarios where they should rely on observations can be achieved by using simulation to produce additional training data. Using modern generative models' capacity to create realistic but unobserved situations as supplementary data for real-world training sets can be effective, if used correctly. A test that evaluates the effectiveness of using simulated data to enhance both the consistency of causal models and their resistance to distribution shifts shows that using actual experiences to retrain models can increase their resistance to unexpected events, even when these experiences include plausible but unusual situations. Using simulated data can also lead to more flexible and adaptable models, compared to using random events, or no events at all, in terms of their ability to handle unexpected events in both their trained and untrained conditions. However, Using simulated data to retrain models may cause their trained data vulnerabilities to become more pronounced, as well as their flexibility to adapt, in some instances. Using simulated diversity to handle unexpected events can be seen both philosophically and analytically, if used carefully.

Using magnetron sputtering, we synthesized epitaxial Fe-Graphite (FG) structures on graphene/Cu(111)/Si substrates across a range of growth temperatures from 550 to 650 Celsius. Aspherical pentagonal and triangular unit cells comprise the FG structure. Higher temperatures favour a specific arrangement of units in the 111 plane of the Si substrate, while lower temperatures result in distinct configurations. Temperature variations significantly influence the thickness, density, and surface morphology of the FG structure. We explain the phenomenon by attributing it to the altered stability of the $\delta$ and $\gamma$ Fe-Graphite phases caused by the differing mobilities of the Si substrate's steps. We propose that the $\gamma$ phase, which has a higher density than the $\delta$ phase, becomes more prevalent at higher temperatures due to the increased number of step nucleation sites on the Si substrate. This research has significant implications for understanding the mechanism of epitaxial growth and the relationship between the $\delta$ and $\gamma$ phases, which can be applied to synthesizing other materials on Si substrates.

We introduce the concept of $ \mathbb{Z}_3 \mathbb{Z}_9 $-linear codes and examine the structure of $ \mathbb{Z}_3 \mathbb{Z}_9 $-linear codes in a systematic approach. We investigate the rank bounds for $ \mathbb{Z}_3 \mathbb{Z}_9 $-linear codes, providing lower and upper limits to assess their rank. We derive an infinite family of $ \mathbb{Z}_3 \mathbb{Z}_9 $-linear codes with rank bounds, as well as optimal rank bounds achievable by $ \mathbb{Z}_3 \mathbb{Z}_9 $-linear codes, in an effort to construct codes that minimize rank while maintaining desirable properties. We also explore the projection of $ \mathbb{Z}_3 \mathbb{Z}_9 $-linear codes in their third component, offering insights into their structural characteristics. We analyze the ideal generated by images of $ \mathbb{Z}_3 \mathbb{Z}_9 $-linear codes, as well as their generator and parity check matrices.

The single-to-multi-label (S2M) sampling technique converts a single label
classification problem into a multi label one. This approach is appealing as
it allows for the creation of rich multi label data from a single label
annotation at a reduced cost. In this study, we employ a neural network based
generative framework that integrates a utility estimator and a generator. The
utility estimator evaluates the potential usefulness of transforming a single
label into a multi label instance for the base classifier, while the generator
is responsible for creating the corresponding multi label instance. By training
this system alongside the base classifier, we achieve accurate single and multi
label classification performance. Experimentation on five public datasets
initially annotated with single labels and later expanded with multi label
versions, shows a 6.8% cost effectiveness in achieving the same accuracy
as the multi label classifier trained on fully annotated data. The results
also show that the S2M sampling based generative framework delivers strong
performance at 80% less annotation cost.

Given any base category, there is a way to assign a "weak natural transformation" to any pair of functors that are derived from an adjunction, which can be characterized in terms of the projection maps of a certain constructed category. For single-object cases, this constructed category reduces to the bar construction associated with the adjunction in question. The "weak strictification" of an adjunction is closely related to this constructed bar. We observe that the constructed bar is equivalent to the bar construction of the "derived" adjunction when certain conditions are met, which is relevant in the context of homotopical considerations. For specific examples involving algebraic structures like monoidal categories, lax monoidal categories, and 2-categorical structures, this constructed bar turns out to be precisely the bar construction of the underlying lax monoidal category or 2-category, respectively.

An analysis of the 2010 GeV gamma-ray data from M87 was conducted using the MAD model, which needed to account for observed high-energy radiation. A key factor in this analysis was electron heating, which we calculated using a plasma simulation to understand its impact. The heating rate found in this study was not uniform across all particles, with some experiencing up to ten times the average rate. The distribution of heating rates also matched expected patterns. The heating rate's influence on the effectiveness of the MAD model varied significantly, with rates 0.1 and 10 times the standard showing clear effects on the model's ability to reproduce observed gamma-ray radiation. A waterfall pattern in the radiation resulted from the heating current driven by a magnetic field, which could help differentiate between models in future studies.

Accurately identifying cardiac abnormalities through sound recordings is crucial for non-experts to detect issues and refer patients to cardiologists, particularly in areas with high rates of heart disease. However, low-quality audio recordings often contain significant noise, hindering the effectiveness of current automatic detection methods. We propose a novel end-to-end audio enhancement and classification framework that simultaneously reduces background noise and classifies cardiac abnormalities. By employing an attention-based substructure to weigh the importance of frequency components in the enhanced audio, our model achieves superior results on both synthetic and real datasets containing various types of background noise. Furthermore, evaluations indicate that our method provides enhanced quality assessments when compared to several established metrics.

Recent advancements in mobile and wearable devices with rich sensors have significantly boosted their capability to automatically identify physical activities. While initial algorithms worked well with homogeneous datasets, their performance declined when applied to real-world scenarios due to the need for intensive data annotation and model training on each device. To address these limitations, FedHealth, a federated learning-based wearable activity recognition system, was developed. This system allows for high-accuracy activity recognition without large data annotation costs or model training on individual devices. Evaluations on extensive heterogeneous datasets involving simulation and hardware devices showed that FedHealth outperforms the state-of-the-art transfer learning method by up to 10% in performance and avoids model training on each device. Furthermore, FedHealth surpasses the average performance in the complex scenario and offers significant improvements over the transfer learning approach.

In portfolio management strategies, historical data plays a crucial role in modeling market dynamics, allocating capital to assets, and executing transactions. Once a portfolio strategy is established and a model is in place, assessing the strategy's effectiveness becomes the most challenging task. This research focuses on assessing the robustness of portfolio allocation strategies by examining how optimization techniques, specifically utility and multi-objective optimization, affect performance metrics under simulated scenarios. The study utilizes machine learning to predict the returns of reference portfolios, without considering risk, and employs linear regression to allocate portfolios, comparing utility and multi-objective optimization approaches to a benchmark that selects portfolios based on predicted returns. The research reveals that utility and multi-objective optimization have negligible effects on performance metrics, indicating the necessity for non-linear risk modeling. Additionally, the study finds that risk-aversion in utility optimization does not enhance performance, indicating that simple single-objective optimization fails to reflect real-world market conditions. The results imply that linear risk allocation is ineffective and suggests exploring other performance indicators, such as return distributions, for more accurate robust evaluation.

Recruiting involves multiple rounds of interviewing, which can be efficiency-enhanced through the use of algorithms to schedule interviews and assemble panels. This paper describes a comprehensive system that integrates several components: an initial round of interviewing, further rounds of interviewing, interview scheduling, and panel assembly. The author focuses on developing a re-usable framework for the first three components using the Datalog language, which allows for customizable and scalable solutions. The system is demonstrated through the implementation of the initial round of interviewing using Proverber, a Datalog system with indexing capabilities. With access to over a billion rows of data, the author shows how to efficiently schedule interviews and assemble panels by leveraging the power of parallel Datalog.

This paper focuses on a class of equations known as LSDEs in a setting with time variation. It provides existence results for solutions to these equations and investigates the optimal strategy for an agent in a financial market that may be influenced by a slow-changing or stochastic environment. It shows that the agent's payoff is maximized in a deterministic setting for all parameters, and in the case of a simple diffusion, the payoff is strictly greater for non-trivial parameters. It also establishes similar findings for a market with a stochastic environment.

We examine the asymmetric leptoquark pair production mechanism in scenarios where a single leptoquark type is created, with one new high-energy particle and one recovered from a lower one, particularly for cases where the leptoquark has both scalar and complex vector properties. Calculations of the cross section for this process were carried out in the leading order of perturbation theory, using an optimization technique known as phase space mapping. A significant advantage of this asymmetric pair production over the traditional radiative leptoquark production is that our calculations do not require incorporating the spin of an incoming proton. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the phase space mapping technique, we computed the cross section for the process involving a scalar 36-3 leptoquark, and the results can be applied to current and future experimental searches at hadron colliders.

The two selected bursters, ICGJ15256.5+5309 and ICGJ1745.0-3958, detected by the IMAGINE survey as extremes of a normal star formation sequence, provide an opportunity to investigate the accuracy of extreme bottom-up extrapolations. The ratios of CI line emissions in these galaxies can be used to detect the presence of low-density molecular wind or a circumgalactic gas reservoir that may not be accessible through traditional spectral fitting methods. The two CI* doublets at 492.16 and 809.20 MHz, however, offer a constraint on extreme scenarios by yielding ratios inconsistent with scattering in the extreme radiation fields of these galaxies. The bursters' optical spectra reveal that the actual conditions of ionization are more complex, requiring the consideration of neutral gas components, possibly in the form of outflows, that traditional spectral fitting methods may fail to detect. The optical equivalent widths of high-ionization lines are unusually large, possibly due to the extended lifespans of H II regions in these galaxies. The unusual characteristics of ICGJ15256.5+5309, however, necessitate the inclusion of low-density gas components, similar to what is observed in other extreme cases, and may be used to predict the characteristics of a type II supernova, ultimately revealing the origin of its radio burst.

In the context of a $u$-twin edge percolation model, where the probability of bond retention is set to $\text{p}=(1-\delta)/\text{d}$ in the Cayley graph, with specific constraints on errors and distance, we set out to find the largest possible radius $r$ for two metric balls whose largest overlapping region is sufficient to include a specified set, and subsequently to identify this intersection. To achieve these objectives, we utilized the Zhiang-Shelah decomposition as a key tool.

The accuracy of approximate formulas for pixelated power spectra, which is relevant to PTA experiments, has been evaluated to determine how closely they match the results of precise numerical integrations. When error margins are expected to be substantial, particularly at high frequencies, a new method for calculating pixelated power spectra is proposed that can provide smaller errors. The effectiveness of this approach has been tested in multiple scenarios including simple rectangular frequency windows, circular windows, and those used by the LISA experiment. Furthermore, assumptions previously made to simplify pixelated power spectra calculations, which are often based on large pixel area approximations, have been reviewed and refined to better account for edge effects within the projection matrix.

We investigate the time evolution of second-class particles in the asymmetric simple exclusion process (ASEP). By leveraging the connection between ASEP and tau functions within the Toda lattice hierarchy, we derive an expression for the joint distribution of these particles in terms of Toeplitz determinants. By applying the "diagonal" approach, we obtain explicit formulas for these determinants, allowing us to analyze the asymptotic (time) behavior of second-class particles in certain initial configurations of ASEP. In particular, we find that the dominant contribution to these determinants arises from a subdominant branch of the elliptic function essential to the product measure dynamics of ASEP. As a result, we establish the asymptotic (time) distribution of the position of second-class particles in the open periodic ASEP model, achieving this by evaluating the determinants on the torus.

Finding a suitable model that accurately represents available data is crucial in science and engineering.  In optimization and systems identification, methods are employed to minimize discrepancies between simulated data from proposed models and observed data, yielding model parameters that reduce this gap.  However, simply obtaining the best fit is insufficient; it is also vital to ensure the resulting parameters are biologically feasible.  This is where feasibility-focused fitting comes into play, an approach that integrates the requirement of biological feasibility with the objective of finding the best fit.  We will this concept in relation to fitting ordinary and stochastic differential models, and we will illustrate feasibility-focused fitting with simulations of the Lassa fever transmission dynamics.

An effective non-rigid pendulum model that accounts for mass loss and the release of a well has been utilized to analyze the complex dynamics of atom-molecule conversion and the emergence of instabilities in a quantum system under the influence of Feshbach resonances. By applying this model, we have developed an exact method to track the evolution of the molecule fraction over time, as well as the instantaneous and final distribution of atoms and molecules. Moreover, it enables us to investigate the influence of parameter changes on the system's behavior, including the investigation of the branch of continuous molecules in the pendulum model and the conditions under which molecules can become trapped, as well as the investigation of the effective potential well created by the cosh function, the impact of molecular weight, and the conditions for molecules to escape the potential well.

Our research explores the challenges associated with DNA data storage, focusing on inefficiencies in packaging stored data and the errors that occur during reading reading processes. We address both issues concurrently, treating the reading and packaging processes as inverse functions of each other. To tackle this problem, we introduced a novel method that leverages the unique characteristics of the reading process to create a segmented storage system. This approach simplifies the management of data packages by using primers that are naturally produced during reading to delete specific partitions. As a result, empty partitions are recycled for repackaging data, effectively primers serve a dual purpose for reading and packaging. We evaluated our design process using real reading data, demonstrating that the recycling process can accurately locate data packages and produces no errors in practice. Furthermore, our system enables a more efficient reading process, allowing empty partitions to be recycled for repackaging data.

The PCGA method is introduced to interpolate and predict bathymetry within a river channel using measured flow velocities. By integrating dimensionality reduction from principal component analysis with geostatistical predictions based on cross-semivariograms, the PCGA technique reduces dependence on the range-to-grid-point ratio. A PCGA model was constructed and compared to kriging models using datasets derived from two bathymetry evolution experiments, yielding more accurate estimates of root-mean-square error, especially in areas with limited measurement data. PCGA demonstrates superior performance over kriging in estimating bathymetry changes within the channel, yielding more consistent spatial patterns.

The technique of automatic exposure selection and high dynamic range image composition is essential for image sensors to images that span the full range of dynamic. Nevertheless, the challenge of selecting optimal exposure settings and merging images for high dynamic range composition remains difficult. In this paper, we present a novel end-to-end loss function that effectively secures the optimal exposure settings by endpointing the high dynamic range composition process. The innovation lies in training a neural network to select exposure settings and capture images directly, with a custom loss function that accounts for the merging of correctly exposed images. The network is trained in two stages: initially, we gather a training dataset using a wide range of exposure settings and reassigns the settings if composition quality declines; subsequently, we employ this method to gather a new dataset for use in final evaluation. Experimental results indicate that this approach significantly enhances the performance of exposure-based image composition. The paper also provides a novel training methodology for exposure selection and demonstrates the applicability of high dynamic range composition to real-world scenarios.

The rapid advancement of deep learning technologies has sparked significant interest in applying them to causal learning, yet the diverse array of research approaches can make it challenging to pinpoint the most promising directions. To address this, we present CausalDL, the first framework for organizing methods in causal learning within the context of deep learning. By dissecting the problem, data, and estimation processes, our framework provides a structured way to map the vast landscape of methods. We highlight over 500 representative papers to illustrate the framework's applicability and to pinpoint areas where deep learning in causal learning lags behind traditional methods. Ultimately, our framework can guide researchers in identifying research gaps, a feature we demonstrate by uncovering potential areas where non-neural network methods could be integrated with deep learning. Open-source code for our framework is available online.

In 1993, Madsen and Weiss established a groundbreaking result, describing the coherent operations on the space of symmetric polynomials defined by the K-theory of open manifolds in even dimensions through the O(n)[\beta,\alpha]-valued symmetric polynomials. This breakthrough was initially presented in an infinite dimension setting and later adapted to finite dimensions by Maxime Glachet in 2021. The underlying mechanism of these stability theorems can be traced back to the mechanism of the B-field, a key concept in topology. The B-field's operation can be illustrated by a matrix \begin{pmatrix} \alpha & \gamma \\ -\gamma & \beta \end{pmatrix}, which explains the relationship between \alpha, \beta, and \gamma in topology. The interaction between \alpha and \beta in topology is also reflected in geometry, as shown in the case of complex surfaces in the 4-dimensional manifold setting, where the intersection number of two divisors D_1 and D_2 equals the surface intersection number of their associated Thiemann bundles in the product of the manifold with the complex plane, given by \langle D_1.D_2\rangle_\Omega^{M\times \mathbb{C}^2}=\langle \alpha.\beta\rangle_\Omega^M.\frac{1}{2\pi i}+ \langle D_1.\gamma\rangle_\Omega^M.\beta

This study applies a balancing domain decomposition method, BDDC, with a novel coarse mesh approach derived from multiplying Hecke operators, to solve multilevel BDDC systems efficiently. The analysis reveals that the BDDC method's performance does not degrade significantly across various dimensions and time step sizes when using this innovative coarse mesh approach. Furthermore, numerical experiments with three-dimensional problems confirm the theoretical findings.

The standard Gaussian diffusion model assumes the absence of correlations and heterogeneity, both horizontally and vertically time, both. The presence of these factors can significantly influence each other and result in non-standard diffusion behavior. The aim of this paper is to investigate the effects of self-excitation and heterogeneity on the factors' behavior & to demonstrate that the system exhibits both correlated and heterogeneous diffusion, both in relation to time & each other. To analyze these properties, we use the characteristic function, as it provides the means to extract the means, variances, coefficients of variation, as well as the tail exponents of the distributions involved, which can be found to be fractal in both the time, and lag dimensions. The results provide the means to derive the probability density functions, which can be compared to existing alternative models, which include the generalized Laplace, the gamma, and the chi-square distributions, which provide the means to better understand the diffusion process, which can be described in terms of the time, lag, number of events, and event sizes, which can be found to be relevant in both the, size, number, lag, and event dimensions, which can be compared to the $t$- and the chi-distributions, which provide the means to better understand the diffusion process, which can be described in terms of the time, lag, number of events, and event sizes, which can be found to be relevant in both the, size, number, lag, and event dimensions, which can

We analyze the nonlinear interaction between various couplings of counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator, including the well-known phenomena of self-phase and cross-phase modulation. Our study involves an extensive analytical and computational examination of the nonlinear interaction integral, revealing that the 0-th order Bessel beam exhibits infinite nonlinear coupling in counterpropagating scenarios, whereas the $n$th order beams display analogous boundary that yields infinite coupling. Our research also identifies a boundary where the cross-phase modulation integral surpasses self-phase modulation, both for beams of the same and different orders.

A novel, efficient multiscale enhanced super-resolution group attention network (MSE-SRGAN) has been developed to model turbulent channel flow. This approach leverages a enhanced group attention mechanism to capture both local and non-local dependencies at scale-dependent levels, enabling accurate reconstruction of high-resolution flow fields from lower-resolution data. A Grelu activation network is incorporated into the model to capture a wide range of scale-dependent variations. The MSE-SRGAN exhibits consistent performance improvements over a broad spectrum of Reynolds numbers (p=4,500 to =111,100), with quantitative and qualitative data demonstrating its superior predictive capabilities. By reconstructing turbulent fluctuation profiles accurately with reduced modeling cost, this explicit data-driven modeling approach presents a realistic alternative to traditional closure models.

In today's complex systems, ensuring safety and reliability is crucial when deploying AI. We introduce a new framework called "SafeSpace," which allows researchers to systematically test AI safety by making precise, reversible modifications to the environment's rules without altering the underlying physics or an agent's learned behavior. We applied this method to evaluate safe reinforcement learning algorithms within a social navigation task, focusing on designing a curriculum that gradually introduces more challenging and potentially unsafe scenarios. By combining our incremental approach with algorithms from the field of safe reinforcement learning, we successfully integrated these scenarios. Additionally, we created a new evaluation metric to assess how safely an agent navigates towards its goal, even in the presence of more difficult and less common test cases.

We introduce the notion of DCR graphs, a visual tool for depicting the dynamics of processes that evolve through discrete time intervals. Each component in a DCR graph represents a specific snapshot of the process at a particular point in time, and directed edges indicate how components interact during that period. We then develop methods for computing linear properties of DCR graphs, allowing us to assess characteristics across their entire structure. Our approach leverages a foundational result from literature, adapting it to the context of linear properties and incorporating an efficient algorithm for computation.

We present two primary approaches to extending moduli varieties toward a comprehensive compact form. Initially, we examine the necessity of adding discrete data in order to achieve a comprehensive compactification through the Satake-Baily-Borel method. Next, we provide a detailed comparison between the geometric and Hodge-theoretic extensions of these varieties, demonstrating their equivalence under specific conditions for the underlying variety. Moreover, we investigate the equivalence between extensions for elliptic curves when applying both methods, showing that they yield nearly equivalent results with distinct interpretative meanings in terms of relevant bundles.

The Cosemca project aims to enable the automatic classification of sentiments in languages other than European, for which existing tools provide comprehensive solutions. To achieve this, we developed a model using a transfer learning approach, which can be easily adapted to different languages. Our model was successfully applied to two non-European languages, achieving an average of 77.5% accuracy in identifying the sentiment behind comments. To facilitate the use of our tool by researchers and developers, we made our code and trained models available on GitHub.

This work aims to enhance the accuracy of predicting ICU bed needs for COVID-19 patients by improving the existing regression models. The hypothesis is that examining specific data, like hospital admission attributes, can provide more accurate forecasts of ICU bed requirements. To achieve this, a new model called PolySense was proposed, capable of analyzing multiple sources of information to make more accurate predictions. In the initial stage, PolySense uses a set of ICU bed Proxy variables, representing hypothetical patients with similar characteristics to actual patients. These simulated data are employed in the second stage, where PolySense combines them with real admission data to forecast ICU bed requirements. Experimental results show that PolySense outperforms current methods in estimating bed requirements across various datasets. Furthermore, PolySense is found to generate more efficient allocation plans by focusing on particular admission features. Additionally, it predicts bed requirements with greater accuracy compared to existing methods.

Functor $\sigma$ from the category of simplicial groups to the category of simplicial groups is defined by applying the left exact functor $\pi_1$ to the total derivation functor. This paper proves that the universal bundle functor is in fact right adjoint to the $\pi_1$-functor, indicating that the universal bundle functor preserves monadic structure when restricted to the category of simplicial groups. Additionally, we demonstrate that the category of monads in the category of simplicial groups is equivalent to the category of 2-monads in the category of groups. This result holds for the category of all monads in the category of simplicial groups as well as for the full subcategory of monads that are accessible and preserve certain structural properties.

Currently, Visual Relationship Detection models rely on balanced sample grouping to reach optimal performance. However, achieving a balanced distribution of predicted relationships through proposal sampling on the vast set of potential relationships remains a challenge. We introduce a novel Balanced Proposal Sampling strategy, known as Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), to effectively address this issue. The sampling method is designed to sample negative proposals that the model is likely to relate to an object, given its current prediction. This results in a dataset with a balanced distribution of predicted relationships that aids in efficient model optimization. BNPS model training can be easily integrated into existing VRD frameworks without significant modifications. In comparative studies, the BNPS method outperforms the standard bi-directional CRF-based model by a 2.0 mAP performance increase and significantly outperforms the baseline in a crisper data subset, demonstrating a 6.6 mAP improvement.

Deep observations of the local universe are made easier with the advancement of imaging and spectroscopy in the near-infrared, allowing for the study of star formation, gas distribution, and velocities in star-forming galaxies. These images and spectra are being combined with advanced techniques to reconstruct gravitational potentials, stellar velocities, and stellar masses of distant galaxies. Such data are crucial for understanding how galaxies evolve over time, particularly the significant contributions made by accretion streams. These streams, which consist of both old and young stars, are identified using machine learning to sort galaxies into different categories based on their origin. This paper builds on previous studies by examining the properties of galaxies that are thought to be part of the accretion streams, with a focus on their optical properties, morphological characteristics, and gas content. We also investigate the optical and infrared characteristics of these galaxies to better characterize their populations and compare their morphological and gas properties to those of galaxies that are categorized as having an inside-out evolution path. This analysis is focused on the context of the formation of massive, interacting, and turbulent galaxies at the center of galaxy clusters in a time frame of 1 to 3 billion years from a host galaxy's maturity.
